scientific_findings.finding_label: Mitochondrial oxidant production is source- and state-dependent
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Experimental suppressors and ischaemia models establish source regulation, not dietary effectiveness. These results do not imply that all mitochondrial ROS are harmful or that mitochondrial emission assays isolate gross production.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Experimental suppressors and ischaemia models establish source regulation, not dietary effectiveness. These results do not imply that all mitochondrial ROS are harmful or that mitochondrial emission assays isolate gross production.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Vitamin E protection depends on tissue and stress context
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Vitamin E deficiency and repletion experiments support a protective role for vitamin E in selected mitochondrial membranes. Mitochondrial-GPX4 loss in mice caused retinal lipid oxidation and photoreceptor loss partly ameliorated by vitamin E. Other rat liver experiments did not show the same dependence.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Vitamin E deficiency and repletion experiments support a protective role for vitamin E in selected mitochondrial membranes. Mitochondrial-GPX4 loss in mice caused retinal lipid oxidation and photoreceptor loss partly ameliorated by vitamin E. Other rat liver experiments did not show the same dependence.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Capacity is not benefit from extra intake. Deficiency models, mitochondrial-GPX4 deletion and high supplemental exposure do not establish ordinary-food equivalence, uniform protection across tissues or cognitive benefit. Retinal lipid assays were not measurements restricted to isolated mitochondrial membranes.

scientific_findings.finding_label: SOD2 metal occupancy affects mitochondrial protein injury
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Manganese supports the normal catalytic identity of mitochondrial SOD2. In manganese-deficient or iron-enriched mouse diets, iron-substituted SOD2 acquired prooxidant activity associated with mitochondrial protein oxidation, including complex I.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Manganese supports the normal catalytic identity of mitochondrial SOD2. In manganese-deficient or iron-enriched mouse diets, iron-substituted SOD2 acquired prooxidant activity associated with mitochondrial protein oxidation, including complex I.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is a cofactor-dependent protective role, not control of ROS-generating electron-leak sites. Animal deficiency/iron excess and cellular SOD2 overexpression do not establish benefit from additional manganese in replete people or a safe supplement target.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Manganese supports the normal catalytic identity of mitochondrial SOD2. In manganese-deficient or iron-enriched mouse diets, iron-substituted SOD2 acquired prooxidant activity associated with mitochondrial protein oxidation, including complex I.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is a cofactor-dependent protective role, not control of ROS-generating electron-leak sites. Animal deficiency/iron excess and cellular SOD2 overexpression do not establish benefit from additional manganese in replete people or a safe supplement target.
